title: Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Started, Then Stopped
summary:
About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway. "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen, and yet it stopped," says Nicolas Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system."

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between about 95,000 and 20,000 years ago. At its greatest extent, it stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois, and in some locations its ice was more than two miles thick.

Most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, but one surviving piece remains: the Barnes Ice Cap, an ancient remnant on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, covering an area roughly the size of Delaware. "People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young.

Piecing together the history of an ice sheet is hard, because as glaciers advance they scrape across the land, destroying the traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading. But unlike most glaciers, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. So plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating, which measures carbon-14, a form of carbon that living things absorb from the atmosphere and that breaks down at a predictable rate once an organism dies. By dating enough plants, the team could build a timeline of the ice margin advancing over them.

One note on wording: technically, we are still living in an ice age, the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.
why_it_matters: This discovery shows how strongly humans have changed Earth's climate. A natural ice age was starting, and warming stopped it, which helps scientists understand what our choices mean for the planet's future.
